1.text_clean:
1. Two students investigate the variation with temperature $\theta$ of the resistance $R$ of a copper wire. The plastic covered copper wire is wrapped around a mercury-in-glass thermometer and immersed in a beaker of water.
[Diagram: thermometer with a coil of wire wrapped around its bulb, immersed in a beaker of water]
The students allow the water to cool slowly from 95 °C.
The students measure the resistance of the wire and the temperature of the water at the same instant.
Their results are shown with error bars for $R$. Errors in $\theta$ can be ignored.
[Graph: $R$/Ω (5 to 8.5) against $\theta$/°C (0 to 120); six data points with error bars at about (21, 6.3), (34, 6.5), (49, 7.0), (66, 7.15), (79, 7.5), (95, 7.9)]
(a) The students suggest that $R$ is given by $R = R_0(1+\alpha\theta)$.
(i) Draw a line of best fit for these data that is consistent with this equation. [1]
(ii) Calculate the gradient of your best-fit line. [2]
(iii) Deduce $\alpha$. State an appropriate unit for $\alpha$. [4]

2.text_clean:
2. A small ball is released from rest at time $t = 0$ in front of a vertical ruler. A multi-flash photograph is taken of the ball at $t = 0$ and every 0.050 s from then on.
[Image: vertical ruler marked 1 to 30 cm with images of the ball at about 5 cm (release position at $t = 0$), 6 cm, 10 cm, 16 cm and 24.5 cm]
The distance $s$ fallen by the ball is related to the acceleration $g$ of the ball and $t$ by $s = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$.
(a) Determine $g$ using the photograph. [3]
(b) The percentage uncertainty in $t$ is ±5 %.
Estimate the absolute uncertainty in your value of $g$. [3]
(c) Suggest a suitable value for the maximum duration of the flash. [2]

3.text_clean:
3. P transmits a radio signal to Q. Relative to the Earth's surface, Q is stationary and P moves at a speed of $0.70c$ as shown.
[Diagram: P moving at 0.70c towards stationary Q above the Earth's surface]
(a) State, using Galilean relativity, the speed of the radio signal relative to Q. [1]
(b) Determine, using relativistic velocity addition, the speed of the radio signal relative to Q. [2]
(c) A paradigm shift in science replaced Galilean relativity with the theory of special relativity.
Explain how this paradigm shift was linked to Maxwell's discovery of a set of electromagnetic equations. [1]

4.text_clean:
4. The spacetime diagram ($x$, $ct$) for a space station S shows the worldlines of two clocks (clock 1 and clock 2). Each clock is 2.0 km from S. The spacetime diagram also shows the worldline of spaceship A.
[Spacetime diagram: $x$/km from −2 to 5, $ct$/km from 0 to 10; vertical worldlines of clock 2 at $x = -2$ and clock 1 at $x = 2$; worldline of A from origin through (2, 8); event E at (0, 4)]
(a) (i) Outline how clock 1 and clock 2 can be synchronized with a clock on S. [2]
(ii) Determine, in terms of $c$, the speed of A in the reference frame of S. [2]
(iii) Clock 1 and clock 2 emit separate light signals when A is at (0,0).
Identify, on the diagram, the proper time that elapses between the arrival of the light signals at A. [2]
(b) At event E, spaceship P leaves S to intercept spaceship A. The speed of P is $0.50c$ in the reference frame of S.
(i) Identify, with the letter X on the diagram, the event of P intercepting A. [1]
(ii) State, in seconds, the time of event X for clock 2. [1]
(c) Spaceship A then returns to S.
The spacetime diagram shows the rest frame of A on its outward journey ($x'$, $ct'$) and on its return journey ($x''$, $ct''$).
[Spacetime diagram: $x$, $ct$ axes; A's outward worldline $ct'$ with axis $x'$, and return worldline $ct''$ with axis $x''$ starting at the turnaround point]
An observer in A determines, for the reference frame of S, the time $t_1$ immediately before the change of velocity of A and the time $t_2$ immediately after the change of velocity of A.
(i) Identify, with lines and labels on the spacetime diagram, the difference between $t_1$ and $t_2$. [2]
(ii) Explain how the difference between $t_1$ and $t_2$ arises. [1]

5.text_clean:
5. Muons are formed in the Earth's atmosphere 2.5 km above the surface and then travel vertically downwards at a speed of $0.975c$. The mean lifetime of a muon is 2.2 μs when measured in a frame in which the muon is at rest.
(a) Calculate the mean lifetime of the muon for the reference frame of the Earth. [2]
(b) Muons are detected at the Earth's surface.
Explain, with supporting calculations, why this is evidence for time dilation. [3]

6.text_clean:
6. The graph shows the variation of kinetic energy $E_K$ with $\gamma$ (gamma factor) for a muon.
[Graph: $E_K$/MeV (0 to 450) against $\gamma$ (0 to 5); straight line from (1, 0) to about (5, 425)]
(a) Calculate the rest energy of the muon. [2]
(b) The muon has the same charge as an electron. Deduce the potential difference required to accelerate a muon from rest to a speed of $0.96c$. [2]

7.text_clean:
7. A distant observer observes a spacecraft that is falling freely towards a black hole.
According to an observer in the spacecraft, a light ray enters an observation window of the spacecraft and leaves through a second window directly opposite the first.
[Diagram: spacecraft moving towards the event horizon of a black hole; light ray entering a window perpendicular to the spacecraft]
(a) Explain the difference between the path of the light ray as described by the distant observer and the path of the light ray as described by the observer in the spacecraft. [3]
(b) The event horizon is 300 km from the centre of the black hole.
When the spacecraft is at 100 km from the event horizon of the black hole it transmits a radio signal to the distant observer. The duration of the radio message according to the observer on the spacecraft is 7.5 μs.
(i) Calculate the duration of the radio message as received by the distant observer. [2]
(ii) Calculate the mass of the black hole. [1]

8.text_clean:
8. A flywheel is a rotating cylinder used to store rotational kinetic energy. Energy can be transferred from the flywheel as it slows down.
[Diagram: cylindrical flywheel rotating about its vertical axis]
A flywheel used to store energy has a moment of inertia of $0.072\,\text{kg m}^2$ and a maximum angular speed of $8400\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$.
(a) The rotational speed of the flywheel is reduced uniformly from the maximum speed to $3600\,\text{rad s}^{-1}$ in a time of 9.6 s.
(i) Show that an average power of about 200 kW is transferred from the flywheel as its speed is reduced. [2]
(ii) Calculate the torque acting on the flywheel as it decelerates. [2]
(iii) Calculate the number of revolutions that the flywheel makes as it slows down. [2]
(b) An engineer changes the flywheel design to increase the maximum energy that it can store.
Identify two factors that the engineer can change to do this. [2]

9.text_clean:
9. A fixed mass of an ideal gas is taken through a cycle that consists of three processes:
X → Y: Isothermal compression from a pressure of 0.10 MPa and volume of $1.20\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$ to a pressure of 0.48 MPa
Y → Z: Isobaric expansion
Z → X: Adiabatic expansion to the initial state
(a) Draw, on the axes, the $pV$ diagram for this cycle. X and Y are plotted for you. Numbers are not required on the axes. [2]
[Axes: $p$ against $V$ with points Y (high pressure, small volume) and X (low pressure, large volume) plotted]
(b) Show that the volume of the gas at Y is $0.25\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$. [1]
(c) An algebraic statement of the first law of thermodynamics is $Q = \Delta U + W$.
Data for the cycle are provided in the table.
Process | Q / J | ΔU / J | W / J
X → Y | | | −188
Y → Z | +262 | | +105
Z → X | | | +157
whole cycle | | | +74
(i) Complete the table. Use the answer box below for your calculations. [3]
(ii) Determine the volume of the gas at Z. [2]
(iii) Determine the efficiency of this cycle. [2]
(d) Outline why this theoretical cycle is unsuitable for use in a practical heat engine. [2]

10.text_clean:
10. A swimming pool consists of a large tank above ground that is being filled with water. The water flows into the tank through a pipe of radius 0.13 m at a flow speed of $66\,\text{mm s}^{-1}$.
[Diagram (not to scale): pipe pouring water into a swimming pool tank; small hole in the side wall 0.80 m above the bottom with water escaping]
Density of water = $1000\,\text{kg m}^{-3}$
Viscosity of water = $1.1\times10^{-3}\,\text{Pa s}$
(a) Identify whether the flow of the water in the pipe is likely to be turbulent. [1]
(b) There is a small hole in the side of the tank through which water escapes.
The small hole is 0.80 m above the bottom of the tank and the radius of the small hole is 19 mm. The depth of water $d$ does not change once the flow rate into the tank is equal to the flow rate out of the tank.
Determine this constant value of $d$. [3]
(c) A block of wood floats on the surface of the water.
Outline, with reference to pressure, the origin of the buoyancy force on the block. [2]

11.text_clean:
11. A person rides a recumbent bicycle that has a suspension unit mounted between the saddle and the bicycle frame. The suspension unit supports the mass of the person and consists of a spring with a damping mechanism.
The natural frequency of vibration of the suspension unit is 2.6 Hz.
[Diagram: recumbent cycle with enlarged view of the spring suspension unit]
The suspension unit is damaged so that the spring is undamped.
The bicycle travels over bumpy ground with bumps separated by equal distances of 1.2 m.
(a) Explain why the ride is uncomfortable when the speed of the bicycle is $3.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}$. [2]
(b) The suspension unit is repaired so that the spring is damped.
Describe any changes that the person will notice when riding over the same bumpy ground. [2]

12.text_clean:
12. A real image, four times larger than the object, is formed 0.40 m from a converging lens.
(a) Calculate the focal length of the lens. [3]
(b) The converging lens is replaced by a diverging lens of focal length $f$. The position of the object is shown.
[Diagram: diverging lens on principal axis with focal points $f$ on each side; upright object arrow placed beyond the focal point on the left]
Determine, using a ray diagram, the nature of the image formed. [2]

13.text_clean:
13. (a) (i) Identify the optical components in an astronomical reflecting telescope with Newtonian mounting. [2]
(ii) Explain one advantage that an astronomical reflecting telescope with a Cassegrain mounting has over one with a Newtonian mounting. [1]
(b) In a reflecting telescope with a Cassegrain mounting, the primary mirror has a focal length of 8.0 m. The telescope is used to view a feature on the Moon that subtends an angle of 2.5 mrad at the axis of the primary mirror.
[Diagram: Cassegrain telescope tube with primary mirror at the right, secondary mirror on the principal axis, point X behind the primary mirror; two incoming rays parallel to the principal axis]
(i) Calculate the height of the image formed by the primary mirror. [1]
(ii) The initial paths of two rays parallel to the principal axis are shown on the diagram. Show, by completing the paths of these rays, the formation of the final image at X. [2]
(iii) The secondary mirror is 4.5 m from X. Calculate the focal length of the secondary mirror. [2]

14.text_clean:
14. Light propagates along an optic fibre that has a core of refractive index 1.59 and a cladding of refractive index 1.48.
(a) Show that the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary is approximately 70°. [2]
(b) A ray enters the optic fibre from the air through a core surface that is at 90° to the axis of the fibre.
[Diagram: ray incident from air at angle $I$ to the fibre axis on the flat end face of the core; cladding above and below]
(i) Determine the largest angle of incidence $I$ that this ray can have in the air for total internal reflection to occur at the core-cladding boundary. [2]
(ii) Describe what happens to rays of light with angles of incidence greater than $I$. [1]
(c) The attenuation per unit length in the core material is $5.5\,\text{dB km}^{-1}$.
Estimate the length of the optic fibre that will reduce the brightness of light by a factor of $10^6$. [2]

15.text_clean:
15. (a) Distinguish between mass attenuation coefficient and linear attenuation coefficient as used in X-ray imaging. [2]
(b) Monochromatic X-radiation of photon energy $E$ is used to image a bone fracture in a human leg. The mass attenuation coefficient for the bone is $\mu_b$ and the mass attenuation coefficient for the muscle around the bone is $\mu_m$. The graph shows the variation of $\frac{\mu_b}{\mu_m}$ with $\ln(E/\text{MeV})$.
[Graph: $\mu_b/\mu_m$ (0 to 6.0) against $\ln(E/\text{MeV})$ (−8.0 to 4.0); curve rises from about 1.3 at −6.3 to a peak of about 5.3 at −4.7, falls to about 1.1 near −1, then rises slowly to about 1.8 at 2.6]
Justify, in eV, the photon energy that is most suitable for imaging the bone fracture. [4]

16.text_clean:
16. In a nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) scanner, a patient is placed in a magnetic field formed by combining gradient and uniform fields.
(a) Outline why magnetic fields are used. [1]
(b) Outline how the gradient magnetic field allows the location of a signal from the patient to be determined. [3]

17.text_clean:
17. (a) Outline the differences between open stellar clusters and globular stellar clusters. [2]
(b) Discuss how Cepheid variable stars are used for distance determinations in astronomy. [3]
(c) Galactic dust absorbs light.
Predict the effect that galactic dust has on the estimate of the distance to a Cepheid variable star. [2]

18.text_clean:
18. Data for the main-sequence star 10 Lacertae are provided. $T_\odot$ and $L_\odot$ refer to the temperature of the Sun and to the luminosity of the Sun.
surface temperature of 10 Lacertae = $6.3\,T_\odot$
luminosity of 10 Lacertae = $100\,000\,L_\odot$
(a) Calculate $\frac{\text{radius of 10 Lacertae}}{\text{radius of the Sun}}$. [3]
(b) Show that the mass of 10 Lacertae is about 30 times the mass of the Sun. [2]
(c) Outline, with reference to its mass, the likely final state of 10 Lacertae. [2]

19.text_clean:
19. The galaxy NGC 6251 is 350 Mly from Earth and has a redshift of 0.025.
(a) Show that the NGC 6251 data lead to an estimate for the Hubble constant of about $70\,\text{km s}^{-1}\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$. [3]
(b) (i) Estimate, using your answer to (a), the age of the universe in seconds. [2]
(ii) State the assumption you made in your estimate for (b)(i). [1]

20.text_clean:
20. The Jeans mass $M_j$ of an interstellar gas cloud is equal to $\frac{CRT}{m}$ where:
$R$ is the radius of the gas cloud
$T$ is the temperature of the gas cloud
$m$ is the mass of the particles in the cloud
$C$ is a constant that has the value $6.2\times10^{-13}\,\text{kg}^2\,\text{m}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$.
(a) Outline the significance of $M_j$. [2]
(b) A spherical gas cloud of radius $7\times10^{15}\,\text{m}$ contains particles of mass $3.3\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$ at a density of $5.0\times10^{-19}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}$. The mean temperature of the cloud is 10 K.
Determine the stability of this cloud. [4]

(b) The Planck Space Observatory revealed temperature fluctuations in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation. Outline one consequence of these fluctuations. [2]
